seoDescription: Learn how to build and deploy a no-code AI chatbot directly into WhatsApp using Flowise. This tutorial guides you through creating a sophisticated RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) chatbot capable of answering questions about your business using a knowledge base. You'll see how to set up the chatbot in Flowise, add conversational memory to recall past interactions, and integrate it seamlessly with WhatsApp via the Meta for Developers API and Make.com. By the end, you will have a fully functional WhatsApp AI chatbot that you can monitor and improve.

chapters.description: This chapter introduces the project: building a no-code WhatsApp AI chatbot with Flowise that has conversational memory and can be monitored.

chapters.description: This chapter explains how to access Flowise, either through self-hosting with Render or by signing up for the paid Flowise Cloud service.

chapters.description: This chapter covers creating a new chatflow, adding a tool agent, connecting an OpenAI chat model, and including buffer memory for conversation history.

chapters.title: Creating a Retriever Tool and Vector Store
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to add and configure a retriever tool, an in-memory vector store, and an OpenAI embeddings node for the RAG functionality.

chapters.title: Setting Up and Managing the Knowledge Base
chapters.description: This chapter shows how to create a document store in Flowise to manage the knowledge base, upload a file, and split it into processed chunks.

chapters.title: Connecting and Testing the Chatbot in Flowise
chapters.description: This chapter covers connecting the document store to the vector store, upserting the data, and testing the RAG chatbot within the Flowise UI.

chapters.title: Setting Up the Meta for Developers App
chapters.description: This chapter walks through creating a new app in the Meta for Developers portal and configuring it for the WhatsApp Business API integration.

chapters.title: Configuring the WhatsApp API Connection
chapters.description: This chapter explains how to configure the WhatsApp API, including managing phone numbers and sending a test message to confirm the initial setup.

chapters.title: Creating the Integration Scenario in Make.com
chapters.description: This chapter introduces Make.com as the integration middleware and shows how to create a new scenario that listens for incoming WhatsApp messages.

chapters.title: Testing the Make.com to WhatsApp Connection
chapters.description: This chapter details testing the webhook by sending a message from WhatsApp and configuring a hardcoded response from Make.com to confirm two-way communication.

chapters.title: Integrating Flowise with Make.com via API
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to use an HTTP module in Make.com to call the Flowise chatbot's API endpoint and pass the user's message as input.

chapters.title: Parsing the API Response and Replying to the User
chapters.description: This chapter shows how to parse the stringified JSON response from Flowise, extract the clean text output, and send it back to the WhatsApp user.

chapters.title: Implementing Conversational Memory
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to enable conversational memory by passing a unique session ID, using the user's phone number, in the API call to Flowise.

chapters.title: Finalizing, Customizing, and Deploying the Chatbot
chapters.description: This chapter covers activating the Make.com scenario, customizing the bot's personality in Flowise, and notes the need for a permanent Meta access token.

summary:
## Core Architecture

The solution combines three platforms to create a WhatsApp AI chatbot:
- **Flowise**: Used to build the no-code RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) chatbot, manage the knowledge base, and define the bot's logic.
- **WhatsApp (via Meta API)**: Serves as the user-facing interface, allowing users to interact with the chatbot directly in their WhatsApp application.
- **Make.com**: Acts as the integration middleware, connecting the WhatsApp API to the Flowise chatbot API to pass messages back and forth.

## Building the Chatbot in Flowise

The chatbot is built using a **Tool Agent** that leverages several key components:
- **Chat Model**: **GPT-4o mini** is used for generating responses.
- **Memory**: A **Buffer Memory** node is added to enable the chatbot to remember past interactions in a conversation.
- **Retriever Tool**: This tool allows the agent to fetch relevant information from a knowledge base.
- **Knowledge Base Setup**: Information is provided to the bot via a **Document Store**.
  - A source document (e.g., a Word file with FAQs) is uploaded.
  - A **Recursive Character Text Splitter** breaks the document into manageable chunks.
  - The chunks are loaded into an **In-Memory Vector Store** using **OpenAI Embeddings**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> After setting up the knowledge source, you must click the **Upsert** button on the chatflow to load the document data into the vector store. This only needs to be done once per data source change.

## Integrating with WhatsApp via Meta & Make.com

### Meta for Developers Setup
1.  Create a **Business App** and link it to a **Business Portfolio**.
2.  Add the **WhatsApp** product to your app.
3.  In the **API Setup** screen, you get your API credentials, including a temporary access token and a test phone number.
4.  Add and verify your own phone number to the test recipient list.

> [!WARNING]
> The default Meta access token is **temporary** and expires after 24 hours. You must complete your business verification on Meta to generate a permanent token for production use.

### Make.com Scenario
The integration is handled by a Make.com scenario with the following modules:
1.  **Trigger (`WhatsApp Business Cloud > Watch Events`)**: Creates a webhook URL that listens for incoming messages from WhatsApp.
2.  **Action 1 (`HTTP > Make a Request`)**: Calls the Flowise chatbot's API endpoint.
    - **Method**: `POST`
    - **URL**: Copied from the API button in the Flowise chatflow.
    - **Request Body**: A JSON object passing the user's message from WhatsApp to the `question` field of the Flowise API.
3.  **Action 2 (`JSON > Parse JSON`)**: The response from Flowise is a string, so this module parses it into a structured JSON object.
4.  **Action 3 (`WhatsApp Business Cloud > Send a Message`)**: Takes the `text` value from the parsed JSON and sends it back to the user's WhatsApp number.

## Enabling Advanced Features

### Conversational Memory
To give the chatbot memory, you must pass a unique identifier for each user in the API call.
- In the **HTTP** module's request body, add an `overrideConfig` object.
- Inside `overrideConfig`, add a `sessionID` property.
- Map the **user's phone number** from the initial WhatsApp trigger to the `sessionID` value.

### Customizing Personality
- In the Flowise **Tool Agent** node, click on **Additional Parameters**.
- Here, you can add a **System Message** to define the chatbot's name, role, and personality (e.g., "Your name is Max. You are a helpful support agent for the Oak and Barrel restaurant.").

> [!TIP]
> You can also use the system message to instruct the bot on its response style, such as asking it to include emojis.
transcription:
## Introduction: Building a WhatsApp AI Chatbot

Are you ready to bring your AI chatbot directly into WhatsApp? In this video, I'll show you how to build a no-code chatbot with Flowise and seamlessly integrate it into WhatsApp for instant access. 

Today we're taking chatbot development to the next level by integrating it directly into WhatsApp. Whether you need a single conversational bot or an advanced AI-driven solution, Flowise makes it super easy. There's no coding required either. 

By the end of the video, you'll have a chatbot that not only integrates into WhatsApp but also remembers past conversations and allows you to monitor interactions for continuous improvement. Let's get started.

## Getting Started with Flowise

There are two ways in which you can access Flowise in the cloud. The first option is to self-host Flowise, and I've already created a video on deploying Flowise to Render, and you'll find a link to that video in the description. Alternatively, you can sign up for Flowise Cloud. This is a paid service, but if you sign up now, you will receive a free trial period. And if you use the link in the description, you will be supporting my channel as I will receive a small commission.

After clicking my referral link, you will be taken to this sign-up screen over here. Simply sign up with GitHub, Google, or your email address. There will be a short wait for your instance to spin up, but afterwards you will receive access to the Flowise dashboard. If you're new to Flowise, you can use it to create all sorts of AI applications, whether you want to create simple conversational chatbots or advanced multi-agent applications.

## Building a Basic RAG Chatbot in Flowise

So if you would like to learn more about Flowise, then I highly recommend checking out my full Flowise playlist on my channel. First things first, let's switch over to dark mode as this white background is blinding me. Then under chatflows, let's click on add new. Let's then click on save. Let's give our flow a name, like WhatsApp chatbot. 

We can use Flowise to create some advanced chatbots, but for this tutorial, we'll just create a simple RAG chatbot that can answer questions about our business. So for my business, I created this simple FAQ document in Word that simply contains questions and answers about my business. And what we want is to create a chatbot that will be able to answer questions about our business using RAG. 

Let's start by adding a new node to the canvas and let's add an agent. And under agents, let's add a tool agent. Let's add an AI model to this project by clicking on add nodes. Then under chat models, let's add the chat OpenAI node and let's connect this model to our tool agent, like so. For this chat OpenAI node, let's go ahead and select our OpenAI credentials. Then let's select our model by changing it to GPT-4o mini and we'll change the temperature to 0.7. 

We want our assistant to be able to recall information from the conversation history so that the user can ask follow up questions. For that to work, we need to add a memory node. Let's go to add nodes, then under memory, let's add the buffer memory node and let's attach it to the tool agent as well.

## Creating a Retriever Tool and Vector Store

For the tool, we will add a retriever tool which will allow the agent to fetch information from a knowledge base. So under tools, let's add the retriever tool and let's attach this retriever tool to the tool agent as well. Let's give the tool a name like 'restaurant info'. For the description, let's say 'use this tool to fetch information about the restaurant'. 

This retriever tool takes in a retriever as input. So let's go to add nodes, then vector stores and let's add the in-memory vector store and let's attach it to the retriever tool. Then this in-memory vector store requires a document as well as an embeddings function. Let's start with the embeddings function. So under add nodes, let's go to embeddings and let's add the OpenAI embedding node and let's attach it to the vector store. For the embeddings node, let's also select our credentials and I'll leave the model as the default value. 

All we need to do now is to attach our knowledge base to this document input. Now there are many different ways to add information to the vector store. First, under add nodes, you can go to document loaders and view all the different integration options over here. So you can add PDF documents, plain text, Word documents, you can scrape websites, etc.

## Setting Up and Managing the Knowledge Base

But what I prefer to do is to go back to the dashboard, then go to document stores, then let's create a new document store. Let's give it a name like 'oak and barrel'. Let's click on add, then let's click on the document store that we just created. Let's click on add document loader. Now I'll select the file on my PC, then under text splitters, let's select the recursive character text splitter. Let's change the chunk size to something like 400 with a chunk overlap of 50 and let's click on preview chunks. Right, and we can see that the document was chunked into 13 smaller documents. 

Let's go ahead and process this. Fantastic! We now have a super simple way to manage our knowledge base. If we wanted, we could add additional document loaders to this document store, but this is all I need for now. Let's go back to chat flows, let's open up our chatbot, then let's go to add nodes, document loaders, and let's add the document store node. We can then select the document store that we just created, and let's attach this document store node to the vector store.

## Connecting and Testing the Chatbot in Flowise

Great! We're actually done with our chatbot. Let's save it. After saving the flow, you will notice this green button will appear, and this will allow us to upsert the data from that document store into our vector database. We only have to execute this once. Let's click on upsert, and we can see that the 13 records from the document store were now loaded into our in-memory vector store. We can now test out our chat, so let's ask it something about the business, like 'what are your specials?'. And we do get this response back, and we can see that the restaurant info tool was indeed used to retrieve that context. 

Now that we have an awesome chatbot that we can run in Flowise, we now want to move on and integrate this chatbot into WhatsApp. That's why you came here after all.

## Setting Up the Meta for Developers App

So let's go over to developers.facebook.com, and let's click on My Apps. You will need to sign in with a Facebook account, and afterwards you should see a dashboard similar to this. Let's start by creating a new app. On this screen, you will be asked to select a business portfolio. When this is your first time running through this process, you won't have any business portfolios in this list. But in order to use WhatsApp with this application, we do need to create a business portfolio. You might see a link on the screen that will allow you to create a business portfolio, but if you don't see anything like that, then you can go over to business.facebook.com, and on the left hand side, click on this drop down, and then click on Create a Business Portfolio.

After you've created a business portfolio, you can simply refresh this page, and you should see your business portfolio show up in this list. Then select your business portfolio, and click on Next. On this screen, let's click on Other, and let's click on Next. On this screen, let's click on Business, which will give us access to WhatsApp. Let's click on Next. Let's give our app a name, like Flowise Chatbot, enter your email address, and again, select your business portfolio. Let's click on Create App. Great, we're making good progress. On this screen, find WhatsApp, and click on Set Up.

## Configuring the WhatsApp API Connection

From this screen, you can either click on Start Using the API, or on the left hand side, click on API Setup. This screen might look intimidating, but I promise you, it's not that bad. We will use this access token in a minute, but when we scroll down, we can see a From number, as well as a To number. The From number is the mobile number that your users will see when they receive messages from your chatbot. Then the To number is a test number which we can use while building this application. 

Initially, when you click on this drop down, you won't see any numbers here, and to add your number, simply click on Manage Find Number List. Then enter your phone number, and then the rest of the process is quite simple. Once you've added your number, simply select it from this list, and if you click on Send Message, you should receive this Hello World message to WhatsApp, indicating that it is working. But of course, if we send a reply, nothing will happen.

## Creating the Integration Scenario in Make.com

Now let's have a look at how we can receive messages from the user, and send responses back to the user as well. For this, we will use Make.com. You will find the link to Make.com in the description of this video, and if you use that link, you will be supporting my channel as well. We will use Make.com to effectively glue Flowise and WhatsApp together. Go ahead and sign up for a new account, or log in. 

After signing in, click on Scenarios, then click on Create a New Scenario. Then let's add a new app by searching for WhatsApp Business Cloud, and let's select Watch Events. From the webhook, let's click on Add. Let's give our webhook a name. I'll just call mine 'Flowwise YouTube Tutorial'. Then under Connection, click on Add. Then give your connection a name. Again, I'll just call mine 'Flowwise YouTube Tutorial'. Then for the permanent token, go back to Meta, then copy the temporary access token, and paste it into this field. Then for the WhatsApp Business Account ID, let's copy the WhatsApp Business Account ID from over here. And let's paste it into Make. Let's save this. 

Let's also enter a verify token, and this can be anything you want. I'll just call mine 'Flowwise'. Under Events, let's listen for messages, and let's click on Save. Now let's copy this webhook that was generated, and let's go back to Meta. Then let's click on Configuration. Within Configuration, we can now paste in that webhook URL, and let's enter the verify token, which I called 'Flowwise'. And then let's click on Verify and Save. Within the webhook fields, scroll down to Messages, and enable this toggle over here. This is all we have to do to start receiving messages from WhatsApp.

## Testing the Make.com to WhatsApp Connection

Let's go back to Make.com. Let's click on Run Once. Make is now listening for messages from WhatsApp. So let's go back to WhatsApp, and let's send any message. I'll just send Hello. And if we go back to Make, we can see that we received the message. And if we go to Messages, and let's scroll down within Messages, let's click on Text, and here we can see the message 'Hello'. 

Now that we're receiving messages from WhatsApp, we can now do a whole bunch of cool stuff. As an example, let's send a hard coded response back by adding a new module. Let's click on WhatsApp Business Cloud, and let's click on Send a Message. Select the connection that you created earlier. And for the sender ID, we'll select the test number. And for the receiver, let's click on Messages. And let's add the sender phone number. Let's scroll down. And for the message type, let's select Text. And for the body, I'll simply enter 'Hi, how are you?'. Let's save this. Let's click on Run Once. Then back in WhatsApp, let's send 'Hi'. And look at that. We received the response from Make. Great.

## Integrating Flowise with Make.com via API

Now what we want to do is pass the message from the user to our Flowise chatbot, this guy over here, and then take the response of the chatbot and send it back to the user. Thankfully, Flowise makes it incredibly easy to integrate with these chatbots. When we click on this API endpoint button, we can see many different integration options over here. What we're interested in is this curl option over here, which gives us this URL and some additional parameters. 

Let's copy the URL. So it's everything from HTTP up until the end of these characters. And in Make, let's add a new module. So let's click on Add a Module. And let's search for the HTTP module, which will allow us to call the Flowise endpoint. Under HTTP, let's select Make a Request. And let's paste in that Flowise URL. Let's change the method to Post. Let's also add a header. And we can see exactly which values to pass in by copying this header value over here, which is Content Type. And for the value, let's also copy this Application JSON section and add it over here. 

Now for the body type, let's select Raw. For the Content Type, let's select Application JSON. And for the request content, we can actually copy the example provided by Flowise, like so. And let's paste it into this field. This is simply a property called Question with a value of, 'hey, how are you?'. Now, obviously, we don't want to hardcode this value over here, but instead we want to pass in whichever message the user sent. So on the left, let's click on Messages. Let's open up text. And let's add this body value over here. And be sure to add these within these double quotes. Let's click on OK.

## Parsing the API Response and Replying to the User

Let's test this out. So I'm going to click on Run once. In WhatsApp, let's say, 'hey'. And back in Make, we can see that this Flowise executed successfully. And if we look at the response from the HTTP module, we can see in the output, this data structure with the text, 'hello, how can I assist you today?'. And a whole lot of other data as well. Also, if we go back to Flowise and under Settings, if we go to View Messages, we can also see the conversation that was just sent to Flowise. 

Now let's see how we can pass this response from the AI model back to the user via WhatsApp. Now, of course, we could open the WhatsApp module and simply grab that output from the model. So instead of this hardcoded value, let's go to the HTTP output. Let's go to data. In fact, let's add this data value over here. Let's click on OK. Let's click on Run once. Back in WhatsApp, let's say, 'hey, again'. And we do get a response back. But this is really not very helpful. All we want is the value of text, not all this other crap as well. 

Now, unfortunately, this data value is this long, messy string of values. And all we really want is the value of text. So what we need to do is take the string value and pass it into a structure where we can selectively grab the values that we need. Let's select Add a Module. Let's go to JSON. And let's select parse JSON. Now, for the JSON string, we can actually add this data value. And this will split the string up into properties that we can use. Let's click on OK. 

So let's run this again. I'll just say, 'hey, again'. Now, if we have a look at the output of this JSON module, we can see that we now have these individual values coming through. So we've got text, the message ID, et cetera. So now, in the WhatsApp Business Cloud module, all we need to do is I'm actually going to delete this data entry over here. And now from the JSON parse module, we can add the text, like so. 

Let's give this a spin. Let's click on Run once. And this time, we should receive a proper message. Let's say 'hello'. And look at that. We now get the AI's response back.

## Implementing Conversational Memory

However, we can still greatly improve this chatbot by adding memory to it as well as a personality. But first, if you do enjoy this video, then please hit the Like button and consider subscribing to my channel for more Flowise content. 

Let's ask a question about our business. What are the current specials? And of course, I shouldn't forget to click on Run once. I'll just select Use Existing Data, and we do get a response back. So our RAG chatbot is definitely working. Now, let's have a look at adding conversation memory to this chatbot. If I say something like, 'my name is Leon', we do receive a response. But if I then ask it, 'what is my name?', our chatbot will tell us that it actually does not know our name. And that is because it's got no view of the conversation history. Thankfully, this is super easy to set up as well. 

So what we can do is use the user's phone number to uniquely identify that user and then return all the previous messages that were sent by that user. That way, the chatbot will be able to answer follow-up questions and recall information about the user. This is really simple to set up. Let's double-click on the HTTP module. And in the request content, let's add a few more things. I'm just going to move these curly braces. And at the end of question, let's enter comma and below question, let's enter `overrideConfig`, then colon, then opening and closing curly braces, and then a property called `sessionID`, colon. And now we can specify a unique ID for this user. And we can use the user's phone number for this. So under messages, let's add the sender number like so. And let's click on OK. Right. Let's click on run once. I'm actually going to clear this chat and let's see if our memory works. First, I'll say, 'hey', we do get a response back. Let's say, 'my name is Leon'. And now let's ask it, 'what is my name?'. And look at that. Our chatbot remembered my name.

## Finalizing, Customizing, and Deploying the Chatbot

And of course, if we go back to Flowise and view messages, we will be able to view the conversations that are linked to the user's phone numbers. Now that our chatbot is working, we can go to Make and turn on scheduling. And we can set it to 'immediately as data arrives'. Now we don't have to click on 'run once' every time we want to chat to our chatbot. Let's also save this. Then let's test this out by sending, 'hey', and I get a response back immediately. Fantastic.

Another improvement we can make to our chatbot is to go back to Flowise. And within the tool agent, we can click on additional parameters. Here we can set the behavior of our model. Like let's give it a name. Something like: 'Your name is Max. You work as a customer support agent for a restaurant called Oak and Barrel.' And just for fun, let's say something like, 'include emojis in your responses.' Let's save this flow. And in WhatsApp, let's try this out. Let's enter, 'Do you sell steaks?'. And we get our response back, which also includes emojis. Wonderful. 

Now at the moment, we are using a temporary access token within Meta. And this token will expire after 24 hours. Now I'm not going to cover the process of verifying your business on Meta, but there are plenty of other videos on YouTube that will take you through that process. But I hope that you do find this video useful nonetheless, as these WhatsApp chatbots can be extremely valuable to yourself or your customers. 

If you want to learn how to build advanced, multi-agent applications within Flowise, then check out this other video over here.
